paragraphs.heading: A reaction written as symbols
paragraphs.text: A chemical equation is shorthand for a chemical reaction, built from element symbols and chemical formulas. The reactants, the substances you start with, go on the left. The products, the substances the reaction makes, go on the right. An arrow points toward the products to show which way the reaction runs, and plus signs separate the substances on each side. Jean Beguin drew the first one in 1615.

paragraphs.heading: The numbers in front
paragraphs.text: A formula can have a number placed before it, called the stoichiometric coefficient. It says how many entities of that substance, such as molecules, take part in the reaction. When no number is written, the coefficient is taken to be 1.

paragraphs.heading: Notes on the arrow
paragraphs.text: Extra information can sit on the arrow itself. A capital delta (Δ) or a triangle means heat is supplied, and hν means light is supplied. The acid or base the reaction needs as its medium can be named there, or simply written as H⁺ or OH⁻, and temperature, pressure and catalysts are shown the same way. This keeps minor substances off the two sides, makes the kind of reaction easier to see, and lets equations be chained together, which helps when showing reactions that happen in several steps.

paragraphs.heading: Why equations must balance
paragraphs.text: A chemical reaction involves no nuclear reactions, so every element comes through it unchanged. That means each side must show the same number of atoms of each element. The total electric charge must match on both sides too. An equation that meets these rules is called balanced, and you balance it by choosing suitable coefficients.

paragraphs.heading: Balancing by inspection
paragraphs.text: Simple equations can be balanced by trial and error, a method called inspection. Give the most complicated substance a coefficient of 1, then fill in the other coefficients one at a time until every element has equal atom counts on both sides. If fractions turn up along the way, multiply all the coefficients by their lowest common denominator to clear them. Finally, check the result, for instance confirming that both sides hold 1 carbon, 4 hydrogen and 4 oxygen atoms.

paragraphs.heading: Balancing with algebra
paragraphs.text: Another route turns the problem into a system of linear equations that can be solved with standard mathematics. Setting every coefficient to zero always solves it, but that answer is useless. If any other solution exists, there are infinitely many, and each of them balances the equation. The preferred answer uses whole numbers, mostly positive, that share no common divisor larger than one.
